question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Savannah?
body:
## Direct Answer
You find a fractional CRO in Savannah through three practical channels: fractional-executive marketplaces and RevOps talent networks that vet part-time revenue leaders, warm referrals from your local investor, banking, and SaaS founder circles, and targeted LinkedIn outreach filtered by title, geography, and industry fit. Expect to pay a monthly retainer for one to three days a week rather than a full-time salary, and prioritize proven revenue-turnaround experience over physical proximity, since most fractional engagements run hybrid or fully remote.

Savannah's revenue-leadership market is thinner than Atlanta's or Charlotte's, so the winning move is to widen your search radius to the broader Southeast and Coastal-Georgia corridor while keeping onsite cadence negotiable. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer gives a growing company senior go-to-market horsepower — sales, marketing, customer success, and RevOps alignment — without the ~$300K+ all-in cost of a full-time hire. Below is exactly where to look, how to vet candidates, what to pay, and how to structure the engagement so it actually moves revenue.

## What is a fractional CRO and when does a Savannah company actually need one?
A fractional CRO is a seasoned revenue executive who works with your company part-time — typically one to three days per week — owning the entire go-to-market engine across sales, marketing, and customer success. Unlike a consultant who advises and leaves, a fractional CRO carries a number, builds the operating rhythm, hires and coaches the team, and stays accountable for pipeline and bookings. They embed in your leadership meetings, sit in on deals, and rebuild your forecasting and comp plans, but they do it on a fraction of the time and cost of a full-time chief.

For a Savannah business, the trigger is usually one of a few moments. You've crossed roughly $1M to $10M in revenue and your founder-led selling has plateaued. You have reps but no repeatable process, or a marketing team generating leads that sales can't convert. You're preparing for a raise or a sale and need clean revenue metrics and a defensible growth story. Or you have the budget for senior GTM leadership but not the deal flow to justify a permanent CRO salary plus equity. If any of those describe you, fractional leadership is the pragmatic bridge — you get the strategic clarity now and can convert to full-time later once the model is proven. To pressure-test whether the role fits your stage, see the diagnostic framework at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-readiness.

The other honest reason Savannah founders choose fractional: local supply. The metro's economy skews toward logistics, ports, manufacturing, tourism, and a growing but still-young tech and services scene. Career revenue chiefs who've scaled SaaS or B2B services from single-digit to mid-eight-figure revenue are simply rarer here than in a major hub. Fractional engagements let you tap that talent from anywhere while keeping the option of periodic onsite time.

## Where do I actually find fractional CRO candidates near Savannah?
Start with the channels that pre-filter for the exact profile you want, then layer in referral and direct outreach. The highest-signal sources are the fractional-executive marketplaces and revenue-talent networks — these platforms vet operators, publish track records, and match you to people who have done fractional work before (which matters, because doing it well is a distinct skill from being a great full-time CRO). Complement that with your warm network, which in Savannah is unusually powerful because the business community is tight and referrals travel fast.

Here is the search flow that works, from broadest reach to most-targeted:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Define the mandate and budget] --> B[Fractional executive marketplaces]
    A --> C[Warm referrals from local network]
    A --> D[LinkedIn targeted outreach]
    B --> E[Shortlist three to five candidates]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Structured vetting and reference checks]
    F --> G[Paid trial engagement]
    G --> H[Full fractional retainer]
```

**Fractional and RevOps talent networks.** National marketplaces such as Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Continuum, Go Fractional, and Pavilion's talent community specialize in placing part-time revenue and go-to-market executives. These are the fastest path to a vetted shortlist because they carry operators who already run fractional practices and can start within weeks. Filter by industry adjacency (SaaS, B2B services, logistics tech, manufacturing) rather than by zip code.

**Warm referrals inside Coastal Georgia.** Ask the people who see revenue leaders in action: your commercial banker, your CPA and law firm, other founders in your space, and the local ecosystem builders. The Savannah Economic Development Authority (SEDA), The Creative Coast, and the Savannah Area Chamber of Commerce all convene founders and operators and can point you toward fractional talent working locally. A referral from someone who has watched a candidate deliver is worth more than any profile.

**LinkedIn targeted outreach.** Search titles — "Fractional CRO," "Fractional VP Sales," "Interim Chief Revenue Officer" — filtered to Savannah, Atlanta, Charleston, Jacksonville, and the broader Southeast. Many fractional operators explicitly list "Fractional" in their headline and openly take new clients. A short, specific message describing your stage, ARR band, and the outcome you want gets high response rates because these operators are actively business-developing.

Widening geographically is not a compromise — it's the point. Charleston and Jacksonville are each under three hours away, Atlanta is a short flight, and a strong operator two states away who runs a quarterly onsite cadence will out-deliver a mediocre local hire every time. For how to weigh proximity against fit, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/local-vs-remote-fractional-exec.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire the wrong one?
Vetting a fractional revenue chief is different from vetting a full-time one, because you're buying focused impact on a clock, not a multi-year relationship. You want proof they can diagnose a revenue problem fast, install a system, and transfer that capability to your team so the engine keeps running when their days taper. Screen for pattern-matching, not résumé prestige — the question is whether they've fixed a revenue problem shaped like yours, at your stage, in a comparable motion.

Anchor your evaluation on evidence, not vibes. Ask every candidate to walk you through a specific engagement: what the revenue looked like when they arrived, the two or three levers they pulled, the metrics that moved, and how long it took. Strong operators speak in specifics — pipeline coverage ratios, win-rate deltas, sales-cycle compression, net revenue retention — and they'll tell you what didn't work. Then check references with operators who reported to them or hired them, and ask the one question that matters: "Would you hire them again, and for what specifically?"

Use this scorecard to compare candidates on the dimensions that predict fractional success:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Candidate] --> B[Stage fit at your ARR band]
    A --> C[Motion fit sales led or product led]
    A --> D[Documented revenue outcomes]
    A --> E[Systems and RevOps rigor]
    A --> F[Coaching and team transfer]
    A --> G[Fractional experience and availability]
    B --> H[Weighted fit score]
    C --> H
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
```

A few red flags to weed out early. Be wary of the candidate who only wants to sell strategy decks and won't touch the CRM, comp plan, or pipeline reviews — fractional CROs earn their retainer in the operating cadence, not the offsite. Be cautious of anyone who over-commits on days across many clients; a person spread across six retainers can't give you real attention. And discount generic playbook talk that isn't grounded in your specific motion, buyer, and price point. For a full interview framework and question bank, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/vetting-fractional-revenue-leaders.

## What does a fractional CRO cost in the Savannah market?
Fractional CRO pricing is structured as a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week, and it varies widely by the operator's pedigree and the scope of the mandate. The honest answer is that rates are set by the individual and the market, not by a published fee schedule, so treat any single number as a range to negotiate rather than a fixed price. What's consistent is the shape of the deal: a recurring monthly retainer, an initial term of three to six months, and a scope that maps to a specific number of working days.

The economics are the reason fractional works. A full-time CRO in a mid-market company commands a substantial base salary plus variable comp, equity, and benefits — an all-in cost that a sub-$10M company often can't justify. A fractional arrangement gives you a slice of that same caliber of leader for the days you actually need, which is why the model has spread so fast among growth-stage companies. You're paying for judgment and system-building, concentrated into the hours that move the needle, and you scale the commitment up or down as the business changes.

Structure the commercial terms to protect both sides. Define the mandate in writing — the outcomes, the cadence, the days per week, and what "done" looks like at 90 and 180 days. Start with a paid trial or a short initial term so both parties can confirm fit before committing to a longer runway. And clarify the endgame up front: many fractional engagements are explicitly designed to hand off to a full-time hire the fractional CRO helps you recruit, so agree early on whether you're renting leadership permanently or bridging to a permanent seat. For a breakdown of retainer structures and how to model the ROI, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-cost-model.

Whatever the number, judge it against the cost of the status quo. A stalled sales team, a leaky funnel, and a founder buried in deals they should have delegated all carry a real price. If a fractional CRO compresses your sales cycle, lifts win rates, and frees the founder to run the company, the retainer usually pays for itself well inside the initial term.

## How do I structure the engagement so it actually delivers?
The engagement design matters as much as the person. The best fractional CRO relationships share a common architecture: a short diagnostic phase, a prioritized fix list, an operating cadence the fractional leader owns, and a deliberate capability transfer to your team. Skip the diagnostic and you get generic playbooks; skip the transfer and revenue slides the moment the engagement ends. Build both in from day one.

Begin with a 30-day diagnostic. Give the fractional CRO access to your CRM, your last few quarters of pipeline and bookings, your comp plans, and your team, and ask for a written assessment: where the revenue is leaking, what the two or three highest-leverage fixes are, and what the 90-day plan looks like. This phase alone often surfaces problems founders have felt but couldn't name — misaligned incentives, a broken lead-to-opportunity handoff, forecasting that's fiction. From there, the fractional CRO installs the operating rhythm: weekly pipeline reviews, a real forecast, a clean comp plan, and clear metrics that everyone reads the same way.

The cadence is where the value compounds. A good fractional CRO runs your revenue meetings, coaches your reps and managers in live deals, and holds the team accountable to the numbers — that consistency is what turns a plan into results. Insist on that operating discipline in the agreement, and insist on documentation: the playbooks, dashboards, and process docs the fractional leader creates should stay with you. The whole point is that when the engagement winds down or converts to full-time, the revenue engine keeps running because the system, not just the person, was installed. To align the whole go-to-market team behind that system, see the RevOps alignment guide referenced across the PULSE library.

## Related questions
### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A consultant advises and hands you a report; a fractional CRO owns a revenue number, runs the operating cadence, coaches the team, and stays accountable for results part-time. You're buying execution and accountability, not just recommendations.

### Can a fractional CRO work fully remote for a Savannah company?
Yes. Most fractional engagements run hybrid or fully remote, with periodic onsite visits for kickoffs, quarterly planning, and key deals. Prioritize proven revenue-turnaround experience and motion fit over physical proximity.

### How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?
Most run three to twelve months, often structured as a three-to-six-month initial term with renewal. Many are explicitly designed to bridge to a full-time CRO the fractional leader helps you recruit and onboard.

### Should a pre-revenue startup hire a fractional CRO?
Usually not. Fractional CROs deliver most when you already have some traction — reps, leads, or repeatable deals — that needs a system. Very early-stage companies are typically better served by a fractional VP of Sales or founder-led selling first.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?
Commonly one to three days per week, scaled to your needs and budget. The commitment often starts higher during the diagnostic and build phase, then tapers as the operating rhythm and team mature.

## FAQ
**What does CRO stand for?**
CRO stands for Chief Revenue Officer — the executive who owns the entire go-to-market engine across sales, marketing, and customer success, accountable for the company's total revenue and growth.

**Is a fractional CRO cheaper than a full-time hire?**
Yes. You pay a monthly retainer for the specific days you need rather than a full salary, variable comp, equity, and benefits, which makes senior revenue leadership accessible to growth-stage companies that can't justify a permanent chief.

**What size company should hire a fractional CRO?**
Typically companies roughly in the $1M to $10M revenue range that have some traction but have outgrown founder-led selling and need a repeatable, scalable go-to-market system without the cost of a permanent CRO.

**How is a fractional CRO different from a fractional VP of Sales?**
A fractional CRO owns all revenue functions — sales, marketing, and customer success — and the cross-functional strategy that aligns them. A fractional VP of Sales owns the sales team and quota specifically. Choose the CRO when the whole go-to-market engine needs alignment.

**Where can I find fractional CROs if none are based in Savannah?**
Widen your search to Atlanta, Charleston, Jacksonville, and the broader Southeast, and use national fractional-executive marketplaces and LinkedIn. Remote and hybrid engagements are standard, so a great operator elsewhere with periodic onsite time is a strong option.

**How do I measure whether a fractional CRO is working?**
Track leading and lagging revenue metrics agreed up front — pipeline coverage, win rate, sales-cycle length, bookings, and net revenue retention — reviewed against a 90-day plan. You should see process installed and metrics moving within the first quarter.

**Can a fractional CRO help me raise capital or prepare for a sale?**
Yes. A common mandate is cleaning up revenue metrics, building a defensible forecast, and tightening the growth story ahead of a fundraise or exit, which materially strengthens how investors and acquirers value the business.

**Do fractional CROs sign non-competes or work with competitors?**
Reputable fractional operators manage conflicts explicitly and will disclose their client roster. Put confidentiality and non-conflict terms in the engagement agreement, and confirm they aren't serving a direct competitor in your market and segment.
